title: How to Stop a Roof Vent or Vent Cap From Rattling and Banging in the Wind
question: My roof vent (or its cap) rattles and bangs loudly whenever it's windy. How do I figure out which vent is making the noise and quiet it for good?
summary: A wind-rattling roof vent is almost always a loose hinged damper flap, a backed-out mounting screw, or a worn wind-driven turbine/cap — all fixable once you find the exact noisemaker. This guide helps you pinpoint the source and quiet each type, with a clear line on when roof height or a gas flue makes it a pro job.

commonCauses.cause: A loose or warped damper flap inside a bathroom/kitchen exhaust hood vent that flutters and slaps when wind pushes back through the duct
commonCauses.quickCheck: On a windy day, stand under the vent indoors (or at the wall hood) and listen — a light tick-tick-slap that matches gusts points to the spring-loaded backdraft flap, not the cap itself.

commonCauses.cause: Backed-out or missing mounting screws/nails letting the whole vent flange vibrate against the roof deck
commonCauses.quickCheck: From the ground with binoculars (or carefully on a ladder at the eave), look for a vent that visibly shudders or a lifted edge in gusts; a low-pitched bang usually means metal flapping on metal or deck.

commonCauses.cause: A turbine (whirlybird) vent whose bearings are worn or dry, so it wobbles, squeals, or clunks as it spins
commonCauses.quickCheck: Watch the turbine spin in wind — a smooth quiet spin is fine; visible wobble, a rhythmic squeak, or a stop-start clunk means dry or failed bearings.

commonCauses.cause: A loose plastic or metal cap on a plumbing vent stack or furnace/water-heater B-vent that lifts and clatters
commonCauses.quickCheck: Identify which pipe noises track the wind; a B-vent's rain cap can rattle on its standoffs. Anything serving a gas appliance flue is a pro item, not a DIY tighten.

commonCauses.cause: An undersized or unsecured cap/hood that resonates — the part is attached but acts like a reed in the wind
commonCauses.quickCheck: If screws are tight and the flap is fine but it still hums or buzzes only at certain wind speeds, the cap geometry itself is the culprit and likely needs replacing with a heavier, baffled model.

fixes: Locate the exact vent first. On the next windy day, walk the attic and the exterior and match the noise to one vent — bath fan hood, range hood cap, turbine, or pipe cap. Fixing the wrong one wastes a roof trip. Do all roof-level inspection from the attic, a stable ladder at the eave, or the ground with binoculars; do not walk a steep, wet, or high roof.

For a fluttering damper flap (most common): from inside, remove the interior grille of the bath/kitchen fan and check the backdraft flap, or at the exterior hood lift the louver. Make sure it swings freely and seats flat. Add a small self-adhesive felt or foam bumper where the flap meets the housing so it closes quietly, or replace a warped flap or louvered cap with a new one (about $10-$25). Do not glue, tape, or block the flap shut — it must still open to vent moisture or grease, or you risk mold in the duct.
For any loose roof flange, fastener, flashing, turbine, or cap, photograph it from the ground and use a licensed roofer. Do not climb onto the roof to tighten, lubricate, seal, or replace it.

If the suspected vent serves a furnace, water heater, fireplace, or other fuel-burning appliance, stop using the appliance when vent damage, soot, gas odor, or a CO alarm is present and contact the gas utility or a licensed combustion professional. Do not alter the cap or flue.

For plumbing vents, never seal or cap a stack that was originally open — codes require the vent to stay open, and capping it can siphon traps and let sewer gas indoors. Only re-secure a cap that is meant to be there.
After any fix, wait for the next windy day to confirm the noise is gone before assuming you're done — vents can have more than one loose part.
diyVsPro: DIY is limited to identifying the sound from the ground or a finished interior grille and cleaning or replacing an accessible interior exhaust-fan damper exactly as its manual directs. Do not use a ladder or enter an unfinished attic for this guide. A roofer handles every roof-mounted part; a licensed combustion professional handles every fuel-appliance vent.
typicalCostUSD: DIY: $5-$25 for felt/foam bumpers, sealant, and screws; $10-$60 for a replacement flap, cap, or turbine. Pro: roughly $150-$400 for a service call to re-secure or replace a single roof vent, more if flashing or decking repair is needed.
timeEstimate: 15-45 minutes to locate and quiet a reachable flap or tighten a flange; 1-2 hours to swap a cap or turbine. Add time for waiting on a windy day to confirm both the source and the fix.
safetyNote: Roof work is a leading cause of serious home-DIY falls. Never go on a steep, wet, icy, or tall roof — do all roof-level work from the attic, a wall hood, or a stable ladder at a low eave, or hire a pro. Do not tighten, seal, or cap any furnace, water-heater, or other gas-appliance flue; an improperly altered flue can cause carbon-monoxide backup — that is a licensed pro's job. If a rattle comes with any gas or sewer smell, soot, or signs of leaking, stop and call a professional.
toolsParts: Binoculars (to spot the noisy vent from the ground)
Self-adhesive felt or closed-cell foam weatherstrip bumpers
Replacement backdraft damper flap or louvered vent cap (if needed)
